spe-01.title: Diversity and Special Education
explain: **Special education** is education that supports learning and daily life by matching each student’s educational needs. Every student learns in a different way, and when those differences call for special support at school, special education designs that support. This process is theoretical study for understanding the basic ideas of special education, regardless of teacher certification or field practicum. It does not deal with the diagnosis or classification of any particular student.

**Educational needs** point to what a student must have more of in lessons and the environment in order to reach a goal. Needs are not determined by a student’s attributes alone. The same student may need less help in a classroom with large-print materials and more help in a noisy hallway. So special education looks at **the point where the student and the environment meet** rather than trying to fix the student.

Two ways of explaining are worth distinguishing. The **individual-centered view** locates the source of difficulty within the student, while the **environment-centered view** holds that difficulty arises when environmental barriers meet the student’s characteristics. Actual discussions usually consider both. There is no agreement that either one alone is correct.

explain.alt: Four horizontal bars. From the top: reading long texts (the longest bar, labeled ‘high’), small-group conversation (medium length, labeled ‘moderate’), moving around the classroom (short bar, labeled ‘low’), and math concepts (short bar, labeled ‘low’). A line below says that the same student needs different support in each area.
explain.caption: Fictional student Haneul’s support needs by area

explain: As the figure shows, one student’s needs differ from area to area. Assuming that a student who needs a lot of support in one area needs it in every area is a mistake.

**Person-first language** is a habit of naming the person first and placing the characteristic afterward, such as “a student who has a disability” rather than “a disabled student.” Some communities, however, prefer identity-first language that puts the characteristic up front. So the safest principle is less about memorizing rules and more about **asking for and respecting the preferred terms of the people concerned**.

Some expressions are also best avoided. Labeling a person by a single trait (“that child is ○○”), portraying someone as pitiable (“suffering”), or depicting someone only as a hero (“overcoming a disability”) hides the other sides of that person.

When reading long passages, Haneul easily loses track of the line, so reading materials with wider line spacing and read-aloud support help. On the other hand, Haneul needs no particular help understanding math concepts.

The teacher does not summarize this as “Haneul is a child who struggles with reading,” but writes, “Haneul is a student who creates good stories, and materials with wider line spacing help when reading long passages.” Both strengths and needs are visible, and the parts that could change with the environment are revealed.

spe-02.title: Universal Design for Learning
explain: **Universal Design for Learning** (UDL) is an approach that designs lessons from the start so that learners with diverse needs can use them. It resembles building a main entrance that everyone uses from the outset, rather than adding a ramp beside the stairs later. Opening several routes at the design stage helps more students than revising a lesson afterward for one student.

This approach is often introduced through three principles.
- **Multiple means of engagement**: Support learners’ reasons for learning and how they sustain interest and effort, in several ways. Offering choices or widening the range of task difficulty are examples.
- **Multiple means of representation**: Present content in several ways. Adding pictures and spoken explanations to text is an example.
- **Multiple means of action and expression**: Provide several ways for learners to show what they understand. Letting learners choose among writing, speaking, or drawing is an example.

explain.alt: Three boxes side by side. The left box is Engagement: why learn, motivate interest and effort in several ways. The middle box is Representation: what to see, present content in several ways. The right box is Action and expression: how it shows, let learners demonstrate understanding in several ways. A line below says the goal stays the same while several routes are prepared.
explain.caption: Three principles: why, what, and how

explain: The three principles are a way of creating several routes to the same goal. They do not mean lowering the level of the goal. For example, keep the goal “explain the conditions plants need to grow” as it is, and let learners choose whether to explain in writing, in speech, or with drawings.

It is also useful to know the nature of UDL. This design does not replace all individual support, and even with broad design some students may still need additional support. Nor does adding many concrete tools mean good design. The key is first to decide which barrier you aim to remove, and then to select methods that fit it.

- Engagement: Choose between experimenting directly with a flashlight and observing with photographs.
- Representation: Explain the experiment in writing, and also guide with pictures and speech.
- Action and expression: Show results by writing sentences, saying them briefly, or drawing them.
The goal is the same in all three places. Only the routes differ, so each student can choose the route that fits where their barrier lies.

spe-03.title: Instructional Support: Accommodation and Modification
explain: Two terms are often confused when providing learning support to students: accommodation and modification. **Accommodation** changes the methods and the environment so that students reach the same goal and the same standard. **Modification** changes the goal, the expected level, or the content itself. In English-speaking contexts, the distinction is widely drawn with the words accommodation and modification. Usage varies somewhat across countries, regions, and documents, so it is important to check what is actually changing rather than relying on the word alone.

explain.alt: A diagram in two columns. The left column is titled Accommodation: the box says the goal stays the same while the method changes. Examples below: extending test time, showing text in large print. The right column is titled Modification: the box says the goal or the expected level itself changes. Examples below: reducing the amount of content covered, setting an easier goal.
explain.caption: Does the method change, or the goal?

explain:
**Examples of accommodation** commonly cited are the following.
- Extending the time for a test or assignment.
- Enlarging the print or reading the text aloud.
- Letting the student answer orally instead of in writing.
In these cases, “what must be known” stays the same, and only “how the student approaches and shows it” changes.

**Examples of modification** include the following.
- Reducing the number of concepts covered in a unit.
- Setting a separate goal with a lowered expected level for the same topic.
Because modification gives a student goals different from those of other students, it is often emphasized that the decision must be made carefully, after thorough discussion with the student and guardians. This does not mean modification should be used readily when a student needs help. Rather, it means one should first check whether accommodation is sufficient.

The line between the two is sometimes unclear. For example, reducing the reading load is closer to accommodation if it keeps only the core needed to reach the same goal, and closer to modification if the goal itself reduces the content covered. In such cases, judge by asking, “Has what this student must reach in this lesson changed?”
This lesson is a conceptual summary for understanding support, not a guideline for deciding which support suits a particular student.

- While other students compare three materials, Woojin compares two. The amount and level of work expected has changed, which is close to modification.
The teacher first checks whether accommodation is enough, and only for parts that remain out of reach considers modification after discussion with the student and guardians.

spe-04.title: Communication Support
explain: **Communication** is the exchange of meaning. Speech is only one of its methods. Gestures, facial expressions, pictures, writing, and devices that produce sound also convey meaning. In special education, helping students convey their own meaning and understand others, by whatever method, is considered an important task. This lesson only surveys general approaches to support and does not deal with judging or treating any particular characteristic.

Conveying meaning serves several purposes. Examples include **requesting** something, **refusing** and saying no, asking questions, sharing feelings, and greeting others. Students who have difficulty speaking also have all of these purposes. Therefore, one should not assume that because a student cannot speak, the student has little to say.

**Augmentative and alternative communication** (AAC) refers to communication methods that supplement or replace speech. These can be divided into methods that need no tools (gestures, hand signs, facial expressions) and methods that use tools (picture cards, letter boards, devices that produce speech). Which method is appropriate depends on several factors, such as the student’s preference, the setting in which it is used, and the understanding of the people around the student.

explain.alt: On the left, a box for the meaning to convey: I want to rest. In the middle, four method boxes stacked vertically: speech, gesture, picture card, and voice output device. On the right, a box for the listener: check by asking back. The boxes are connected by lines. A line below says there are many methods and the listener confirms the meaning.
explain.caption: There are many ways to convey meaning

explain:
What matters as much as choosing a method is the **listener’s attitude**. Common approaches in conversation include the following.
- Wait long enough for the student to convey meaning.
- Guess the meaning that was conveyed and check it by asking, such as “Do you mean this?”
- Show the choices visibly.
- Let the student know that their attempt has been respected and accepted.

The goal of communication support is not to make the student speak, but to **increase the experiences in which the student’s meaning gets across**. As those experiences accumulate, the student tries to convey a wider variety of meanings in more places.

body: Third grader Doyun rarely speaks and carries picture cards to convey meaning. During class, Doyun handed the teacher a card with a picture of “a place to rest.”
The teacher checked verbally, “You want to go and rest?” When Doyun nodded, the teacher let Doyun go to the resting place, and they decided together what to finish upon returning.
In this scene, the teacher respected the method of the card, checked the meaning by asking, and responded to the request. Doyun is left with the experience of communication succeeding.

spe-05.title: The Idea of Inclusive Education
explain: **Inclusive education** is an approach in which students who need special support for learning learn together with other students in the same school and classroom. The core is that people of different kinds share the same classroom. Terms differ across countries, and a closely related idea is sometimes called “poyong education” (a term for inclusion). This lesson is an overview that introduces several positions in a balanced way, and it does not decide which placement is correct.

Where students learn is not fixed to one place; it can be arranged as a **continuum** according to the degree of support. There are patterns of learning in the general classroom while receiving necessary support, patterns of spending part of the time in a special class, and patterns of learning mainly in a special class or special school. The names and structures differ from region to region.

explain.alt: Five boxes connected by arrows from left to right: general classroom, general classroom with additional support, part-time special class, mainly special class, special school. Below, a line says that the names of the spaces differ by region and that one space is not better than another.
explain.caption: Continuum of learning settings (names vary by region)

explain:
Commonly cited **advantages** from the perspective of supporters of inclusive education are the following.
- There are many opportunities to interact with peers.
- Opportunities open up to access the general curriculum.
- All students experience living with people who are different from them.
- A sense of belonging as a member of the school community can grow.

On the other hand, **concerns and limitations** are also discussed.
- If support staff and materials are lacking, students may sit in the same classroom but actually fail to learn.
- It can be hard for one teacher to meet the needs of many students.
- Being in the same classroom does not automatically create friendships.
- Some opinions hold that a small group receiving intensive support in a special setting is helpful.

A common misunderstanding in this discussion is treating “being placed in the same location” and “learning together” as the same thing. Widely held views hold that the quality of inclusive education depends on **whether support is actually connected** and **whether the student’s own and guardians’ views are reflected**, rather than on the name of the placement.

Na Elementary lacks materials and staff, so students mostly just watch during most of the lesson.

The placement of the two schools is the same, but the learning the students experience is different. This case shows that when evaluating inclusive education, the question to ask is not only the name of the placement but whether support is real.

spe-06.title: Reading a Support Plan
explain: The support a student needs is often organized in a document. Names and formats differ across countries and schools, but generally they contain “current status,” “goals,” “support methods,” and “review.” This lesson is theoretical study for developing the eye to read such documents. It does not teach how to write an actual plan or how to judge students. All examples below are fictional.

explain.alt: Four boxes arranged in a cycle with arrows. From current status (strengths and needs), to goals (small and clear), to support methods (who does what), to review (check whether it works), and back to the start. A line below says that the review leads back to looking at the current status again.
explain.caption: A plan cycles rather than being written once and finished

explain: It is considered desirable that the **current status** records not only weaknesses but also **strengths and interests**, because strengths are the starting point of support. **Goals** are more easily understood the same way by readers when they are written as small, clear, and observable statements. “Reads well” is harder to check than “answers one question about a two-sentence passage.”

**Support methods** record who, where, and in what way support is provided. What was learned earlier, such as accommodations, communication methods, and lesson design, can go here. **Review** records when and by what means the plan will be looked back on. A plan without a review stays the same even when the student changes.

Another important point is the idea that a plan should be created and read **together with the student and guardians**. A plan is widely considered not a good one if the wording in the document is hard to follow or the student’s own decisions cannot be seen.

- Current status: Likes taking photographs and listening to music. In group activities, has difficulty joining in when friends speak quickly.
- Goal 1: States her own opinion at least once during group activities.
- Support methods: Receives a question sheet in advance of the activity. The group takes turns deciding the presentation order.
- Review: After four weeks, Minseo, her guardian, and the teacher meet together to discuss how many times Minseo stated an opinion and how Minseo felt.
In this example, the goal can be checked, the support is concrete, and the review timing and participants are written down. Minseo’s strengths are recorded as well.

spe-07.title: Inclusive Education and the Least Restrictive Environment (LRE)
explain: In Lesson 1, we saw the place where students learn as a **continuum** running from the general classroom to the special school. Then what should decide the point at which a student learns? If standards differ from school to school or from person to person, students with the same needs may end up learning in completely different places. The principle that emerged to answer this question is the **least restrictive environment** (LRE). This lesson is theoretical study for understanding the principle, not a guideline for deciding the placement of any particular student.

LRE is widely introduced as a principle originating in the U.S. Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Its core can be summarized in two statements. First, students with disabilities are educated with children without disabilities **to the maximum extent appropriate**. Second, students are moved to a separate learning environment only when a satisfactory education is difficult to provide even with **supplementary aids and services** in the general classroom. In other words, the starting point is the general classroom, and separation requires a reason. Laws and terms differ across countries, but similar ideas are often used in discussions of inclusive education.

Breaking this principle into steps gives the following.
1. First, examine learning in the general classroom.
2. Consider all the supports that the general classroom can provide (accommodations, aides, assistive technology, co-teaching).
3. Consider learning part of the time in another setting only when there is evidence that the goals still cannot be reached.
4. Review the placement regularly rather than keeping it fixed.
Here “restrictive” does not mean punishment; it refers to **how much the opportunity to be with peers is reduced**.

explain.alt: Three horizontal bars showing each fictional student’s weekly class time out of 30 periods. Gaon: 27 periods in the general classroom and 3 in the special classroom. Narae: 18 in the general classroom and 12 in the special classroom. Dasom: 9 in the general classroom and 21 in the special classroom. Green segments are the general classroom and orange segments are the special classroom (separate learning time).

explain: The figure shows the weekly timetables of three fictional students as proportions. The proportion of time in the general classroom is found by dividing the number of general classroom periods by the total number of periods. For example, 27 out of 30 periods gives 27/30 = 0.9, or 90%. Such proportions are often used as an indicator of the **amount** of inclusion. However, even with the same proportion, the figure alone cannot show what is actually learned in the general classroom or with whom students interact.

Discussions of LRE should also be read in a balanced way. One side holds that the goal should be **full inclusion**, in which all students are in the general classroom. The other side holds that for some students, an intensive small-group support environment may actually be less restrictive. Both positions cite student learning and participation as grounds, and neither is an agreed-upon correct answer.

There are limits and exceptions too. Proportion indicators count only time, so they miss the quality of participation in class. Also, even when students are in the same place, if support is not connected, a substantive separation can occur. Therefore, it is more accurate to read LRE as a principle that asks **whether support is brought to the student first**, rather than as a principle about where the student is placed.

examples.title: Calculating the proportion of general classroom time
body: Condition (fictional): A student’s weekly timetable has 32 periods, of which 8 are spent in a special classroom.
Step 1: Find the general classroom periods. 32 - 8 = 24 periods.
Step 2: Find the proportion. 24/32 = 0.75, or 75%.
Interpretation: The student spends three-quarters of the week in the same class as peers. However, what support is given during those 24 periods should be examined separately.

examples.title: A review order that brings support first
body: Condition (fictional): Student Haram has a record of missing instructions during science experiments and being unable to join the activity.
Step 1: List the supports that can be given inside the general classroom first: a picture sequence chart, pair work, and dividing instructions into short steps.
Step 2: After using these supports for a set period, look at the participation records again.
Interpretation: Following the LRE principle means trying general classroom supports first and using their results as evidence before considering a separate placement.

checks.explanation: LRE starts in the general classroom, considers supports first, examines separation only when there is a reason, and does not keep the placement fixed.

spe-08.title: Present Level of Performance: Writing with Strengths, Needs, and Data
explain: An individualized education program (IEP) is a document that organizes goals and supports for one student. In the support-plan cycle from Lesson 1, the first box was “current status.” In an IEP this is commonly called the **present level of performance**. However, if it begins with sentences like “reading is weak” or “easily distracted,” the goals and supports become vague, because if the starting point is unclear, the destination cannot be set.

A good description of the present level of performance is commonly summarized as containing three elements.
- **Strengths and interests**: What the student already does well and enjoys. This is the starting point for support.
- **Current level based on data**: Concrete figures or behavioral descriptions obtained through observation or measurement.
- **Impact**: How that level affects participation in the general curriculum.
When these three are present, it becomes clear where the goal is moving from and to.

The process of obtaining data can be divided into steps. (1) Choose one skill to check. (2) Measure it several times under the same conditions. (3) Choose a representative value from the measurements. Because a single measurement is affected by the student’s condition on that day, it is often recommended to measure at least three times and use the **median**. The median is the middle value when the values are arranged by size, and it is less affected by a single outlying value.

Let’s read an example closely (fictional). “Minho enjoys picture books and remembers characters in stories well. In three trials of reading a second-grade-level passage aloud for one minute, he read 14, 9, and 11 words correctly (median 11). Classmates typically read about 40 words in the same passage, so Minho has difficulty taking part in activities that involve reading Korean and social studies textbooks on his own.” This paragraph contains strengths (picture books, recalling characters), data (three measurements, median 11), and impact (participation in textbook reading) all together.

Some expressions should be avoided. Sentences that record only a diagnostic label do not say what to teach. Words that judge personality, such as “lazy,” are interpretation rather than observation. Exaggerations such as “always” or “never” often do not match the data. Writing with observed behavior and figures lets everyone who reads it picture the same scene.

Limitations should also be noted. If only measurable skills are recorded, parts that do not show up well in figures, such as the student’s interests, relationships, and wishes, may be left out. Therefore, it is often emphasized that the statements of the student and guardians should be included as well. The examples in this lesson are all fictional and do not deal with how to judge the actual level of a real student.

examples.title: The median of three measurements
body: Condition (fictional): Seoyun’s scores on three dictation trials of 10 items were 6, 3, and 7.
Step 1: Arrange them by size: 3, 6, 7.
Step 2: Pick the middle value. The median is 6 (the mean is 16/3, about 5.3).

Interpretation: One low score of 3 pulls the mean down, but it has little effect on the median. For the present level of performance, write the value with its basis, such as “median of three measurements: 6 out of 10 items.”

examples.title: Rewriting a vague sentence
body: Condition (fictional): The original sentence is “Junwoo can’t do math.”
Step 1: Convert it into observational data about what and how much is done: “Of 10 two-digit addition problems, the 4 without carrying were correct, and the 6 with carrying were wrong.”
Step 2: Add strengths and impact: “Enjoys activities that show numbers with blocks. Has difficulty joining in on classroom problems that require carrying.”
Interpretation: The rewritten sentence naturally points to the next goal (addition with carrying).

checks.hint: Separate what the student likes, the numbers, and participation in class.
checks.explanation: A good present level of performance includes strengths, data, and impact together.

Read 11 words correctly per minute across three measurements
Has difficulty joining activities of reading textbooks independently

checks.hint: Arrange them in order of size and choose the middle value.
checks.explanation: The middle value of 8, 12, and 17 is 12.

checks.explanation: The last sentence combines observable behavior, a figure, and a strength. The others rely on personality judgment, exaggeration, or a diagnostic label.

checks.explanation: The median is the middle value, so it is less affected by an extreme value produced by a one-time change in condition.

Because it is less affected by a single outlying value
Because the result is always larger than the mean
Because measurement needs to be done only once

spe-09.title: Writing Measurable Short-Term and Long-Term Goals
explain: If the present level of performance is the starting point, the **goal** is the destination. However, a goal such as “improve reading ability” cannot be judged as achieved one year later, because each person’s criterion for “improvement” differs. That is why it is most strongly emphasized that IEP goals must be **measurable**.

A frame often used when writing measurable goals is **ABCD**.
- **A (Audience)**: who performs the behavior.
- **B (Behavior)**: the behavior, written with an observable verb such as “says,” “writes,” or “chooses” rather than “understands.”
- **C (Condition)**: the materials and situation in which it is performed.
- **D (Degree)**: how well or how often it must be done to count as achieved.
Example: “Minho (A), when reading a second-grade-level passage aloud for one minute (C), correctly reads 40 or more words (B) on three consecutive trials (D).”

The relation between **long-term goals** (usually one year) and **short-term goals** is like a staircase. Short-term goals divide the distance to the long-term goal into several intermediate points. In a progress graph, a straight line connecting the starting point and the goal, the **aimline**, is drawn to show the expected position each week. The slope of the aimline is as follows. $$\text{기울기} = \frac{\text{목표} - \text{출발 수준}}{\text{기간(주)}}$$

explain.alt: Progress-monitoring graph of the fictional student Raon’s reading fluency. The horizontal axis is weeks (0 to 12); the vertical axis is the number of words read correctly in one minute (0 to 40). Baseline scores for weeks 1 to 3 are 18, 22, and 20; a dotted vertical line between weeks 3 and 4 marks the start of the intervention phase. Scores in the intervention phase, weeks 4 to 9, are 22, 22, 23, 24, 24, and 25. An orange dotted aimline runs from 20 at week 3 to the week-12 target of 38.

explain: Let’s read the figure closely. The median of the three baseline points (18, 22, 20) is 20, which is the starting level, and an aimline runs from week 3 to reach 38 at week 12. The slope is (38 - 20)/(12 - 3) = 18/9 = 2, meaning the number of words should increase by 2 per week. By comparing each intervention-phase point weekly against the aimline, one can judge whether the student is moving toward the goal.

There are limits and cautions in writing goals. If the criterion (D) is set too high, the student repeatedly experiences failure; if set too low, it reduces learning opportunities. Also, if only skills that are easy to measure are chosen as goals, important things such as communication, self-determination, and peer relationships may be left out. Goals gain meaning when they connect to life situations that the student and guardians care about. This lesson is theoretical study for understanding the structure of goal statements, not a guideline for writing an actual IEP.

examples.title: The slope of an aimline and intermediate points
body: Condition (fictional): Starting level 15 words; goal of 45 words after 20 weeks.
Step 1: Find the slope. (45 - 15)/20 = 30/20 = 1.5, that is, 1.5 words per week.
Step 2: Find the intermediate point at 10 weeks. 15 + 1.5 × 10 = 30 words.
Interpretation: “30 or more words after 10 weeks” can be set as a short-term goal. If actual scores stay below this point continuously, review the support methods.

examples.title: Rewriting with ABCD
body: Condition (fictional): The original goal was “Junwoo becomes good at addition.”
Step 1: Specify the behavior and condition: “When given 10 two-digit addition problems that involve carrying, Junwoo writes the correct answers.”
Step 2: Add the criterion: “In weekly measurement, 8 or more of 10 items correct on two consecutive occasions.”
Interpretation: Because there is an audience, an observable behavior, a condition, and a criterion, anyone can judge achievement in the same way.

spe-10.title: UDL Multiple Means and Barrier Analysis
explain: In Lesson 2 we outlined the three principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL). However, knowing the principles does not change a lesson right away. The statement “diversify the presentation” alone does not say what to add to which lesson. This lesson makes UDL concrete through a procedure called **barrier analysis**.

UDL is widely known as a set of guidelines compiled by the U.S. organization CAST. The three principles are explained in connection with three neural networks related to learning.
- **Multiple means of engagement**: why learn. Related to interest, sustaining effort, and self-regulation.
- **Multiple means of representation**: what is learned. Related to how information is perceived and understood.
- **Multiple means of action and expression**: how learning is shown. Related to showing understanding and planning and carrying out actions.
The guidelines are revised over time and the names of detailed items have changed, so this lesson deals only with the structure of the three principles.

Barrier analysis proceeds in the following order.
1. **Clarify the goal**: separate what must be learned in this lesson from what need not be.
2. **Separate means from goals**: if the goal is “explain the conditions of photosynthesis,” long reading and handwriting are means, not goals.
3. **Find the barriers**: anticipate which learners will get stuck in each means.
4. **Include alternatives in advance that fit the principle**: open one more route matched to the principle where the barrier arises.

Let’s read a case (fictional). The goal of a science lesson is “explain three conditions plants need to grow.” The lesson is organized as: read two pages of the textbook, then write on a worksheet by hand. Students who struggle with reading face a barrier of **representation** (reading the text), students whose handwriting is slow face a barrier of **action and expression** (writing), and students uninterested in experiments face a barrier of **engagement**. As alternatives, provide pictures and read-aloud audio along with the text (representation), let students answer by recording speech or by drawing (expression), and let them choose the plant they will grow (engagement). The goal stays the same.

The second step is the most important. If a means is mistaken for a goal, alternatives cannot be given appropriately. For example, if the goal of a Korean-language class is “read a passage aloud accurately,” providing read-aloud audio replaces the goal itself, so it is not suitable for that activity. The same tool can be appropriate or inappropriate depending on the goal.

Limitations of UDL are also discussed. The principles are broad, so practice varies greatly from school to school, and some point out that research designs for measuring effectiveness are difficult. Also, even with a UDL design, some students may still need additional individual accommodations or modifications. UDL is generally understood not as eliminating individual support, but as a design that **reduces the amount of individual support needed from the start**.

examples.title: Barrier analysis in a math lesson
body: Condition (fictional): The goal is “compare the sizes of fractions.” The lesson is 20 minutes of board explanation followed by a 20-item worksheet.
Step 1: Separate means from goals. Listening to the board explanation and solving the 20 items are means.

Step 2: Write barriers and alternatives by principle. Hard to understand by listening alone → fraction-bar manipulatives (representation). Fatigue from too many items → a choice over the number and difficulty of items (engagement). Writing is a barrier → show the answer by arranging the bars instead (expression).
Interpretation: The goal was kept; the routes to the means were widened.

examples.title: Same tool, different judgment
body: Condition (fictional): Whether to use a screen-reading function is being considered for two lessons. The goal of the social studies lesson is “describe the features of a region,” and the goal of the Korean-language lesson is “read a passage aloud fluently.”
Step 1: In the social studies lesson, reading the text is a means. The read-aloud function does not harm the goal.
Step 2: In the Korean-language lesson, reading is the goal itself. The read-aloud function replaces the goal in that activity.
Interpretation: The appropriateness of a tool is determined by the goal, not by the tool itself.

checks.explanation: The three UDL principles are explained in connection with why, what, and how learning occurs, respectively.

What is learned: perceiving and understanding information

checks.hint: The goal comes first and alternatives come last.
checks.explanation: Set the goal, separate the means, then find the barriers and the alternatives.
items: Find barriers that arise in the means

checks.prompt: Case: In a science lesson whose goal is “explain three conditions plants need to grow,” a student’s handwriting is so slow that the student cannot finish the worksheet. Which principle’s barrier is this, and which alternative is appropriate?

It replaces the goal itself, so it is not suitable for this activity

spe-11.title: Types and Hierarchy of Instructional Modifications
explain: In Lesson 3 we distinguished **accommodation** (the goal stays the same and the method changes) from **modification** (the goal or expected level changes). Even when routes are widened from the start with UDL, there are times when a particular student needs changes tailored to a lesson in order to take part. Korean special education literature often refers to such changes broadly as **instructional modifications** and explains them by dividing them into several types. Note that “modification” here is a broader term than the narrower sense used in Lesson 3.

Five categories are commonly introduced.
- **Instructional environment**: seating arrangement, lighting, noise, physical access.
- **Instructional group**: arrangements for learning together, such as pair work, small groups, and peer tutoring.
- **Instructional method**: explanation style, materials, and the way tasks are presented.
- **Instructional content**: the amount or level of content covered.
- **Assessment method**: extended time, response format, evaluation criteria.
The names and number of categories differ slightly among scholars and documents, so here these five categories are used only as a framework for understanding.

It is common to think of **hierarchy** among the types. To keep students from drifting away from the goals of the general curriculum, changes that keep the goal are tried first, and changes that alter the goal are considered later.
1. Change the environment and the group (goal kept).
2. Change the method and materials (goal kept).
3. Change the response format or time in assessment (standard kept).
4. If still difficult, change the amount or level of content (goal changes).
The further down the list, the more the student acquires goals different from peers, so stronger grounds are needed.

Let’s read a case (fictional). In a fourth-grade social studies lesson, “investigating the cultural heritage of our region,” student Eunsol has difficulty with long reading and presentations. First, Eunsol was paired with a friend who is good at organizing information (group). The research materials were changed to cards with photos and short explanations (method). Instead of presenting, Eunsol selected three photos and recorded one sentence of reasons for each (response format in assessment). These three changes did not change the goal, which is to “explain the characteristics of cultural heritage.”

In the same case, if a separate goal had been set for Eunsol, such as “match three names of cultural heritage to photos,” that would be **content modification**. Because this change means Eunsol is evaluated by different criteria from the other students in the class, it is emphasized that it must be thoroughly discussed with the student and guardians and linked to the IEP goals.

There are limitations as well. If changes are excessive, the student may effectively be separated from class activities. Conversely, if necessary changes are not made, learning may not connect even in the same classroom. The hierarchy is best understood not as a fixed rule but as a thinking order: **consider the changes that keep the goal first**.

examples.title: Classifying changes by type
body: Condition (fictional): In a science experiment lesson, the following changes were made for student Taeo. ① Moved to a seat in front of the lab bench. ② Given role cards in a three-person group. ③ The experiment sequence was presented as a picture sequence chart. ④ Results were recorded with photos instead of writing.
Step 1: Check what each change alters. ① seat (environment) ② group structure (group) ③ presentation method (method) ④ response format (assessment).
Step 2: Check whether the goal changed. All four changes keep the goal “explain the results of the experiment.”
Interpretation: This is a case where problems were addressed at the front of the hierarchy without changing the content.

examples.title: Review following the hierarchy
body: Condition (fictional): During a 20-item dictation test, a student tires and stops around item 10.
Step 1: Review changes that keep the goal first. Allow a break and split the test into two sessions (environment and method).
Step 2: If it is still difficult and evidence accumulates, discuss with the student and guardians a content modification that reduces the number of items.
Interpretation: Content modification is not used from the start; prior attempts are used as the basis for the decision.

spe-12.title: Assistive Technology and AAC Access Methods
explain: Even with broad lesson design and instructional modifications, some students need tools in order to take part. Examples include students who have difficulty conveying meaning through speech, holding a pencil, or seeing letters. The tools and services used in these cases are broadly called **assistive technology**. The AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) seen in Lesson 4 is the area of assistive technology that supports communication.

Assistive technology is commonly described in three levels by technology.
- **No-tech**: methods without devices. Gestures, sign language, and pre-agreed signals.
- **Low-tech**: tools that need no electricity or are simple. Picture cards, letter boards, and thick-grip pencils.
- **High-tech**: electronic devices. Speech output devices, tablet communication apps, and screen readers.
A higher technology level is not necessarily better. Because devices can break or run out of charge, it is often advisable to prepare several levels together.

A frame often used when selecting tools is **SETT**. First examine the Student, Environments, and Tasks, then choose the Tools. The key point is that it is not an order of picking a tool first and fitting the student to it. What the student can do and wants, where they use it, and what they must do there determine the tool.

The **access method** for selecting cells in AAC is also important. Pointing directly at the desired cell with a finger or gaze is called **direct selection**. If direct selection is difficult, a **scanning** method is used: the device or a person highlights cells in turn, and the student activates a switch when the desired cell is highlighted. Scanning includes **step scanning**, which highlights one cell at a time in sequence, and **row-column scanning**, which first selects a row and then selects a cell within that row.

explain.alt: A 4-row by 4-column picture communication board (fictional). Row 1: water, meal, restroom, rest. Row 2: play, music, book, outside. Row 3: more, stop, help me, it hurts. Row 4: yes, no, good, dislike. Below, text states that highlighting one cell takes one step. Step scanning highlights cells one by one starting from row 1, column 1. Row-column scanning first selects a row and then a cell in that row.

explain: Let’s compare the two methods using the board in the figure. If highlighting one cell takes one step, then with step scanning, reaching “book” in row 2, column 3 requires passing four cells in row 1 and three cells in row 2, so it takes 7 steps. In row-column scanning, the rows are highlighted in order, row 1 and then row 2 (2 steps), and then columns 1 to 3 in that row (3 steps), for a total of 5 steps. As the number of cells grows, row-column scanning tends to be faster. However, it requires two selections, so the switch must be pressed at the right moment twice.

There are also limits and cautions. Putting frequently used words near the front reduces the number of steps, but frequently rearranging the layout forces the student to relearn where things are. There is also a concern that AAC use will slow speech development, but studies generally report that the evidence that AAC hinders speech development is weak. This lesson is for conceptual understanding and is not a guide for choosing a particular student’s tools.

examples.title: Steps of two scanning methods
body: Condition: On the 4-row by 4-column board in the figure, choose “no” in row 4, column 2. Highlighting one cell takes one step.
Step 1 (step scanning): Pass through the twelve cells in rows 1 to 3, then go to the second cell in row 4, so 12 + 2 = 14 steps.
Step 2 (row-column scanning): Row selection of 4 steps + cell selection within that row of 2 steps = 6 steps.
Interpretation: The difference between the two methods grows for cells lower on the board. Placing frequently used words such as “yes” and “no” near the top reduces the steps under either method.

spe-13.title: ABC Observation and Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA)
explain: When a behavior that disrupts class repeats, a common response is to react to the **form** of the behavior: scold when the student shouts, bring the student back when they leave the seat. However, behaviors of the same form can have different **reasons** depending on the student and the situation. Responding without knowing the reason can actually increase the behavior. The procedure that emerged from this concern is **functional behavior assessment** (FBA). This lesson is theoretical study for understanding concepts, not a guideline for evaluating a real student’s behavior.

The starting point of FBA is the view that a behavior **gets the student something or helps the student avoid something**. The function of behavior is commonly summarized in four categories.
- **Gaining attention**: the attention of teachers or peers, or getting others to talk with them.
- **Gaining items or activities**: a desired toy, snack, or activity.
- **Escape or avoidance**: getting away from a difficult task or an unpleasant situation.
- **Sensory stimulation**: sensations that come from the behavior itself, regardless of social results.
A behavior persists as long as it keeps providing its function.

FBA usually follows these steps.
1. **Operational definition**: define the behavior so that anyone can count it the same way. Instead of “distractible,” use “taps the desk with the palm two or more times.”
2. **ABC observation**: record together the **antecedent** immediately before the behavior (A), the **behavior** (B), and the **consequence** immediately after it (C).
3. **Find patterns**: look for repeated patterns of which antecedents are followed by the behavior and which consequences follow it.
4. **State a hypothesis**: “When (antecedent), (student) does (behavior), and as a result gets (function).”

explain.alt: Five-day ABC observation record of the fictional student Doyun. All six rows show the behavior of tapping the desk. Row 1: dictation begins; result: activity stopped and the student went to the hallway. Row 2: math worksheet handed out; result: the worksheet was taken away. Row 3: teacher working with another group; result: the teacher came over and talked to the student. Row 4: writing task presented; result: task postponed. Row 5: turn to read comes; result: a friend read instead. Row 6: waiting alone while seated; result: the teacher came over.

explain: Let’s read the record closely. All six rows show the same behavior, but the antecedents and results fall into two groups. In rows 1, 2, 4, and 5, the behavior occurred right after a task was presented, and the result was that the task was removed or postponed. In rows 3 and 6, the behavior occurred while the teacher’s attention was elsewhere, and the result was the teacher coming over. So the most frequent pattern is **task avoidance**, and gaining attention may also be operating. This record shows that one behavior can have more than one function.

The hypothesis can be written this way: “When a reading or writing task is presented, Doyun taps the desk, and as a result avoids the task.” A hypothesis is not a conclusion; it is a **guess to be tested**. Later, change the antecedent or the consequence and see whether the behavior changes as predicted, then refine the hypothesis.

There are limits and cautions too. An ABC record does not tell about scenes the observer missed or times when no one was observing. With few records, a chance pattern can be mistaken for a function. The sensory-stimulation function appears regardless of social results, so it is hard to judge from ABC alone. Therefore, interviews, observations across several days, and records from several observers together are recommended.

examples.title: Making an operational definition
body: Condition (fictional): The record card says, “Harin is distractible during class.”
Step 1: Write the observable form: “Lifts the buttocks off the chair and moves more than 1 meter away from the seat.”
Step 2: Set a start and an end: “Count one occurrence from the moment the student leaves the seat until they sit down again.”
Interpretation: With this definition, two observers watching the same scene are more likely to count the same number of occurrences.

body: Condition (fictional): Two students both shout during class. When student Ga shouts, the teacher comes over and soothes Ga; when student Na shouts, the dictation is interrupted.
Step 1: Compare the results. Ga gains the teacher’s attention; Na escapes from the task.
Step 2: Estimate the function. Ga: gaining attention. Na: avoidance.

Interpretation: The same response (for example, sending the student out into the hallway) could make task avoidance easier for Na and increase the behavior. This is why one must look at the function, not the form.

spe-14.title: Competing Behavior Pathway Model and Intervention Design
explain: Having formed a functional hypothesis through FBA, the next question is “what will we change?” **Positive behavior support** (PBS) is an approach that does not stop at reducing problem behavior through punishment. Instead, it creates environments in which the behavior is unnecessary and teaches better ways to obtain the same function. The tool that shows this design at a glance is the **competing behavior pathway model**.

The middle row of the model directly carries over the FBA hypothesis: **setting events** (earlier conditions that raise the likelihood of behavior, such as lack of sleep) → **antecedent** (the immediate trigger) → **problem behavior** → **maintaining consequence** (the function). Two branches are added. The upper branch shows the **desired behavior** the school hopes for in the long run and its outcomes. The lower branch shows the **replacement behavior**, which obtains the **same function** as the problem behavior.

explain.alt: Competing behavior pathway model of the fictional student Doyun. Middle row, connected by arrows: setting event (lack of sleep), antecedent (long writing task), problem behavior (tapping the desk), maintaining consequence (task avoidance). From the antecedent, an upward branch leads to the desired behavior (task completion) and long-term outcomes (praise, free time), and a downward branch leads to the replacement behavior (holding up a rest card). From the replacement behavior, an orange arrow rises to the maintaining consequence, with a note that it is the same result.

explain: Reading the figure closely: a long writing task is still too hard for Doyun, so going straight to the desired behavior of “completing the task” is difficult. The replacement behavior **holding up a rest card** is therefore taught as an intermediate bridge. The key point is that this behavior obtains **the same outcome** as tapping the desk (briefly leaving the task). Only when the function is the same does the student have a reason to choose the replacement behavior over the problem behavior.

In the model, intervention is placed in four positions.
1. **Setting-event intervention**: reduce conditions that raise the likelihood of the behavior, or take the student’s state on that day into account.
2. **Antecedent intervention**: make the behavior unnecessary, such as breaking tasks into shorter parts, offering choices, or giving advance notice.
3. **Behavior teaching**: teach the replacement behavior and the desired behavior.
4. **Consequence intervention**: give the replacement behavior its function immediately (allowing a rest), and make it no longer easy to obtain that function through the problem behavior.
It is often emphasized that a replacement behavior must produce the same result **more easily and quickly** than the problem behavior in order to be effective.

There are limits and ethical concerns too. When a problem behavior no longer obtains its function, the behavior may temporarily increase, a pattern known as an **extinction burst**. Also, if the rest obtained through the replacement behavior continues endlessly, learning opportunities decrease, so plans are needed for gradually returning to the task after a rest and for gradually increasing time on task. PBS aims at both the student’s dignity and quality of life, and it holds as a principle that it does not rely on punitive methods that cause pain. This lesson is for conceptual understanding and is not an actual intervention plan.

examples.title: A replacement behavior for the attention function
body: Condition (fictional): When the teacher is working with another group, student Yuna sings loudly, and the teacher comes over and speaks to Yuna (attention function).
Step 1: Choose a replacement behavior that obtains the same function: raising a hand, or standing a “Please look at me, teacher” card on the desk.
Step 2: Design the antecedent and the consequence together. Before going to another group, give notice, “I’ll come back in 5 minutes,” and when the card is up, respond briefly right away.
Interpretation: For Yuna to choose this route, the replacement behavior must obtain attention more easily and quickly than singing does.

Step 1: Compare the functions. The sticker is gaining an item, while what the student wants is to get briefly away from the task.
Step 2: Revise. Teach a replacement behavior that provides the function of briefly leaving the task, such as a rest-request card.
Interpretation: A replacement behavior can compete only if it obtains the same function as the problem behavior.

spe-15.title: Behavior Measurement and Reading Single-Subject Data
explain: After starting an intervention, the feeling that the student seems better cannot be used to judge progress. One may remember only the good days, or the behavior may not have decreased at all while observation was simply less frequent. That is why PBS and special education research **measure** behavior and often use **single-subject designs**, which graph one student’s changes over time.

Measurement methods are chosen to match the nature of the behavior.
- **Frequency and rate**: count the occurrences. If observation time differs from day to day, convert to occurrences per minute (rate). $$\text{비율} = \frac{\text{횟수}}{\text{관찰 시간(분)}}$$
- **Duration**: how long the behavior continued (for example, crying).
- **Latency**: the time that passes between an instruction and the start of the behavior.
- **Interval recording**: divide the observation time into short intervals and mark whether the behavior occurred in each interval.

There are three kinds of interval recording. **Partial-interval recording** marks an interval if the behavior occurs even once within it, so it tends to **overestimate** the actual amount. **Whole-interval recording** marks an interval only if the behavior continues throughout it, so it tends to **underestimate**. **Momentary time sampling** checks only at the moment each interval ends. Results are expressed as the percentage of intervals marked. $$\text{비율(\%)} = \frac{\text{표시된 간격 수}}{\text{전체 간격 수}} \times 100$$

explain.alt: Partial-interval recording sheet (fictional). Ten minutes divided into 30-second intervals, shown as twenty boxes numbered 1 to 20 in two rows. The boxes marked O are 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 14, and 18; the rest are marked with a dash. Below, O means the student left the seat at least once during the interval, and a dash means it did not occur.

explain: Let’s read the figure. Dividing 10 minutes into 30-second intervals gives 20 intervals. Count the intervals marked for leaving the seat, divide by 20, and multiply by 100 to get the proportion of intervals in which the behavior appeared. Because this is partial-interval recording, the proportion is not the same as “the proportion of 10 minutes spent away from the seat.” If the student left the seat for only 2 seconds within an interval, the entire interval is marked.

Measurements are read on a graph. Before the intervention, the **baseline** (A) and the intervention phase (B) are placed side by side, and three things are compared: **level** (the average height of the values), **trend** (the direction in which values rise or fall), and **variability** (how widely the values are scattered). If the level or the trend clearly changes between the baseline and the intervention phase, the effect of the intervention can be inferred.

The limitations are clear too. An A-B design with only two phases cannot rule out other events in the same period (a new friend, a scheduled event, and so on) as the cause of the change. For that reason, research uses an **ABAB reversal design**, which withdraws and then reintroduces the intervention, or a **multiple-baseline design**, which introduces the intervention at different times across several behaviors or settings, to confirm the effect repeatedly. However, reversal designs do not suit behaviors that cannot be unlearned, such as a skill once learned.

examples.title: Comparing days with different observation times
body: Condition (fictional): On Monday, in a 30-minute observation, there were 6 instances of leaving the seat. On Wednesday, in a 20-minute observation, there were 5.
Step 1: Convert to rates. Monday 6/30 = 0.2 per minute; Wednesday 5/20 = 0.25 per minute.
Step 2: Compare. The count is higher on Monday, but the rate is higher on Wednesday.
Interpretation: When observation times differ, compare by rate rather than by count.

examples.title: Reading level and trend
body: Condition (fictional): The percentage of intervals with task engagement over five baseline days was 30, 25, 35, 30, and 30%. Over five intervention days it was 45, 55, 60, 65, and 70%.
Step 1: Look at the level. The baseline average is 150/5 = 30%; the intervention average is 295/5 = 59%.
Step 2: Look at the trend. The baseline is flat, while the intervention phase rises steadily.
Interpretation: Both level and trend changed, but an A-B design alone cannot rule out other causes.

spe-16.title: Learning Disabilities and Response to Intervention (RTI)
explain: When a student falls far behind peers in reading or math, how can we tell whether the difficulty comes from a lack of support or from a specific difficulty in learning? This question has long been debated. The purpose of this lesson is to understand the logic of two approaches, not to explain how to determine whether a particular student qualifies.

A **learning disability** is generally described as a continuing difficulty in a specific academic area, such as reading, writing, or mathematics, that cannot be explained by overall intellectual disability, sensory impairment, or lack of educational opportunity. A long-used approach is the **ability-achievement discrepancy model**. If academic achievement scores are substantially lower than intelligence test scores, a possible learning disability is considered. Because this method requires waiting until the gap grows large enough, it was criticized as a **“wait-to-fail model.”**

The alternative presented is the **response to intervention model** (RTI). As with the multi-tier support system seen in Lesson 1, every student receives high-quality universal instruction (Tier 1); students whose progress is slow receive small-group supplemental support (Tier 2); and those who still respond poorly receive intensive support (Tier 3). In the United States, after the 2004 reauthorization of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), students’ intervention response data came to be used in identifying learning disabilities, and RTI spread widely. The key idea is to treat **response to high-quality support** as data.

A frequently used judgment framework in RTI is **dual discrepancy**. When a student’s ① **level** (current score) is substantially lower than peers’ and, at the same time, ② **slope** (weekly growth) is also substantially lower than peers’, more intensive support is considered. If only the level is low and the slope is similar to peers’, the student is growing along with the support, and the judgment differs. The slope can be roughly calculated by dividing the change in scores over a period by the number of weeks.

explain.alt: Progress-monitoring graph of the fictional student Raon’s reading fluency. The horizontal axis is weeks (0 to 12); the vertical axis is the number of words read correctly in one minute (0 to 40). Baseline scores for weeks 1 to 3 are 18, 22, and 20; a dotted vertical line between weeks 3 and 4 marks the start of the intervention phase. Scores in the intervention phase, weeks 4 to 9, are 22, 22, 23, 24, 24, and 25. An orange dotted aimline runs from 20 at week 3 to the week-12 target of 38.

explain: Let’s read Raon’s data in this framework. In the intervention phase, the score rose from 22 at week 4 to 25 at week 9, a gain of 3 over 5 weeks, so the slope is 3/5 = 0.6 words per week. The aimline required a slope of 2 words per week. Also, the last five points are all below the aimline. Many schools set decision rules in advance, such as “if several points in a row are below the aimline, change the support methods,” and by this data it is time to review the support methods again. This is not a judgment that the student has a problem, but a **signal to change the support**.

There are debates about RTI too. If the quality of Tier 1 instruction varies from school to school, the same response data carry different meanings. It is also pointed out that it can be hard to tell whether low response is due to a learning disability or to support that did not fit. There are concerns as well that necessary assessments or support must not be delayed by the steps of the RTI process. For this reason, RTI data are generally used together with other information.

examples.title: Comparing dual discrepancy
body: Condition (fictional): Over six weeks, the classmates’ average rose from 60 to 72 words. Student A rose from 25 to 37, and Student B rose from 25 to 28.
Step 1: Find the slopes. Peers 12/6 = 2 per week; A 12/6 = 2 per week; B 3/6 = 0.5 per week.
Step 2: Look at level and slope together. A’s level is low, but A’s slope matches peers. B’s level and slope are both low.
Interpretation: Under the dual discrepancy framework, the candidate for considering more intensive support is B. A is growing within the current support.

Step 2 (RTI): After a first-grade screening, Tier 2 support begins right away and progress is watched weekly.
Interpretation: RTI emphasizes early support, but the quality of support and the decision rules differ from school to school, which is a limitation.

spe-17.title: Support Principles for Autism Spectrum Disorder and Intellectual Disability
explain: Knowing the name of a disability category alone cannot change instruction, because students with the same diagnostic label have their own strengths and needs. Still, knowing the characteristics often mentioned for each category and the support principles helps in anticipating barriers. This lesson is theoretical study that summarizes concepts of support principles. It does not teach diagnostic criteria or judge any student.

**Autism spectrum disorder** is described in the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual (DSM-5) in two domains: ① **persistent differences in social communication and interaction**, and ② **restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities** (including hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input). As the word “spectrum” suggests, the degree and form of support needs vary widely. Some in the autistic community view it as a form of **neurodiversity** rather than a deficit, and this discussion includes several coexisting viewpoints.

Frequently introduced support principles include the following.
- **Visual supports**: information that can be seen, such as a daily schedule or sequence cards.
- **Predictability**: announcing changes in the schedule in advance.
- **Adjusting the sensory environment**: considering stimuli such as noise and lighting.
- **Explicit social skills instruction**: explaining implicit rules concretely.

**Intellectual disability** is generally defined by three elements: ① a substantial limitation in **intellectual functioning**, ② a substantial limitation in **adaptive behavior** (conceptual, social, and practical skills), and ③ onset during the **developmental period**. Adaptive behavior refers to skills for managing daily life, such as money calculation and reading time (conceptual), following rules and forming relationships (social), and dressing and using transportation (practical). Recent definitions tend to understand disability in terms of the **level of support needed**, not IQ scores alone.

A method often used in supporting students with intellectual disability is **task analysis**. A complex skill is broken into small steps taught in sequence, and whether the student performed each step independently is recorded. For example, handwashing can be divided into ① turn on the water, ② wet the hands, ③ apply soap, ④ scrub, ⑤ rinse, ⑥ turn off the water, ⑦ dry with a towel, and ⑧ hang the towel. Progress can then be seen by how many of the eight steps the student does independently. **Community-based instruction**, which teaches in real-life settings, is also introduced as a method that aids generalization.

Limits and cautions: a list of characteristics by category can easily lead to stereotypes such as “all students in this category are like this.” Variation within a category is large, and one student may have characteristics of several categories. Also, diagnostic labels and educational needs do not correspond one-to-one. Support should start from the student’s present level of performance and barrier analysis, not from the diagnostic label.

examples.title: Reading a task analysis record
body: Condition (fictional): Of the eight handwashing steps, the steps student Danbi did independently on Monday were ①, ②, ⑤, ⑥, ⑦, and ⑧.
Step 1: Count the steps done independently: 6 steps.
Step 2: Convert to a proportion. 6/8 = 0.75, or 75%.
Interpretation: The steps that need help are ③ applying soap and ④ scrubbing. The next support can focus on these two steps.

examples.title: Designing predictability
body: Condition (fictional): Because of rain, physical education was changed to indoor activities. Student Gyeoul is recorded as often becoming upset when the schedule changes.
Step 1: On the visual daily schedule, replace the “playground” card with a “gymnasium” card, and show it in the morning in advance.
Step 2: Reorganize the changed sequence of activities again using picture cards.
Interpretation: Predictability and the principle of visual supports were applied together. Whether this was effective should be checked again with records.

checks.hint: Water must come on before the hands can be wet.
checks.explanation: A task analysis divides a skill into small steps in the order they are actually performed.

checks.prompt: A fictional student completed 7 of 10 steps independently in a dressing task divided into 10 steps. What percentage (%) was done independently?
checks.hint: Divide the number of steps done independently by the total number of steps, then multiply by 100.

checks.prompt: Match examples of adaptive behavior with their domains.
checks.hint: Separate numbers and time, relationships and rules, and daily-life performance.
checks.explanation: Adaptive behavior is described as conceptual, social, and practical skills.
pairs: Calculates the price of goods and checks the change
Takes turns with friends while playing

checks.prompt: Plan: “Because all students with autism spectrum disorder are sensitive to sound, they are given earplugs in all classes.” Which judgment is most appropriate?
checks.hint: Recall the meaning of “spectrum.”
checks.explanation: Differences in sensory response are part of the descriptions of autism spectrum disorder, but they vary greatly among students. Support starts from individual data, not from the diagnostic label.
options: Because it generalizes a domain characteristic to all students, it is a stereotype; support should start from that student’s present level of performance and barrier analysis
Since the same diagnostic label should have the same support, it is appropriate
Sensory characteristics are unrelated to autism spectrum disorder
Earplugs are not assistive technology, so they cannot be used

spe-18.title: Support for Sensory Disabilities and Transition Education
explain: For students who cannot see or hear well, barriers to lessons usually arise in the **channels through which information is accessed**. The more information depends on a single sense, such as writing on the board, the teacher’s speech, or video materials, the greater the barrier. Also, preparing for life after school (work, independence, and community participation) is an important task of special education. This lesson covers the principles of support for sensory disabilities together with **transition education**.

Methods commonly introduced for supporting students with **visual impairment** include the following.
- **Braille**: a tactile writing system read with the fingers.
- **Magnification**: enlarged print, magnifiers, and screen-magnification features.
- **Screen readers**: software that reads on-screen text aloud.
- **Orientation and mobility training**: skills for moving safely with tools such as a white cane.
A teacher’s habit of describing pictures or board writing verbally and concretely is also a great help.

Support for students with **hearing impairment** includes sign language interpretation, captions, real-time text transcription, remote microphone systems that transmit the teacher’s voice directly, and seating arrangements where faces and mouths are visible. In addition, some Deaf communities hold a view of **sign language as a language in its own right, and Deafness as a cultural and linguistic identity**. There is a long-standing debate between approaches centered on listening and speaking, approaches centered on sign language, and approaches that use both. It is commonly emphasized that the choices of students and families should be respected.

**Transition education** is education that plans and supports the process of moving from school to adult life. Employment, continuing education, independent living, and community participation are its main domains. The classification of transition programs by **Kohler** is often cited as a framework. It consists of five areas: ① student-centered planning, ② student competency development, ③ interagency collaboration, ④ family involvement, and ⑤ program structure.

At the center of transition education is **self-determination**. Self-determination refers to the ability and attitude to make choices that affect one’s own life, set goals, and reflect on the outcomes. For example, a student who attends their own IEP meeting and personally describes their strengths and desired career is both engaging in student-centered planning and gaining an opportunity to develop self-determination. If adults decide everything in place of the student, no matter how elaborate the plan, the strength needed in adult life is not developed.

Limits and cautions: interagency collaboration is hard to generalize because the kinds and systems of agencies differ by region. Also, if “independence” is understood narrowly as doing everything alone without help, one may miss a life of making choices for oneself while receiving the support one needs. This lesson is for conceptual understanding and is not advice about the career or medical choices of a particular student.

examples.title: Analyzing information channels
body: Condition (fictional): In a science lesson, the teacher shows a video (with spoken commentary) and summarizes it on the board. The class includes one student with visual impairment and one with hearing impairment.
Step 1: Divide the information by the sense it depends on. The video screen and the board writing rely on sight; the commentary relies on hearing.

Step 2: Open one more channel. For the student with visual impairment, describe the screen content verbally and provide the board notes as an electronic file. For the student with hearing impairment, prepare captions and a remote microphone system.
Interpretation: Adding another channel to information that depends on a single sense also connects with the representation principle of UDL.

examples.title: Classifying a transition plan by domain
body: Condition (fictional): High school student Saebom’s transition plan includes the following activities. ① Saebom announces a desired job at a meeting. ② Work experience twice a week at a school café. ③ Linked consultation with a local employment support agency. ④ A guardian takes part in weekend public-transportation practice.
Step 1: Match each activity with a Kohler category: ① student-centered planning, ② student competency development, ③ interagency collaboration, ④ family involvement.
Step 2: Check for missing domains. No program-structure area, which covers school-level policy and resources, is visible.
Interpretation: The classification framework can be used as a checklist for finding areas missing from a plan.

checks.prompt: Match transition activities with the Kohler categories.
checks.hint: Who is the agent, and what is the activity changing?
checks.explanation: Kohler’s categories are student-centered planning, student competency development, interagency collaboration, family involvement, and program structure.
